newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek dig pinpoints cave of playwright Euripides.
newsitem.headline: Greek dig pinpoints cave of playwright Euripides.

text.p: Greek archaeologists say they have located the island cave where the playwright Euripides probably wrote some of his ancient masterpieces, the culture ministry said in a statement on Friday.
Historical evidence has long indicated that Euripides, the latest of three great Athenian dramatists, sought solitude to work in a cave on the island of Salamis near Athens.
Now a clay pot dating from his lifetime and inscribed with his name has been unearthed in a cave at Peristeria in the south of the island.

"The pot with Euripides's name is a unique find which adds to our knowledge of intellectual life in the fifth century BC," archaeologist Yannos Lolos, a professor at the Ioannina University who heads excavations at the cave, said.
Among the works of the reclusive Euripides, who was born in 480 BC, are Medea, Hecuba and the Trojan Women.
"I can picture him sitting at the terrace at the entry of the cave, looking out at the Saronic Gulf and composing his plays," Lolos told Reuters.
Euripides was considered eccentric for his love of solitude at a time when company was greatly valued. Ancient biographers described him as stern, strict and unsmiling.
His dark tragedies reflect some of this brooding character but are also sensitive studies of the human condition and the struggle to control passion and fight the gods.
He was parodied in Aristophanes's comedy, The Frogs, and was criticised by contemporaries for his innovations in tragedy.
Disappointed, he left Athens for the court of King Archaelaus in Macedonia, where he wrote one of his most often-perfomed plays -- the Bacchae. He died in 406 BC.
The culture ministry said the hardest evidence tying Euripides to the cave was the clay pot inscribed with the first six letters of his name.
The pot dates to 440-430 BC and graphologists say the inscription was applied later, around the second century BC, most probably as a votive offer by an admirer of the writer.

"He might have used that pot himself but we may never know for sure," Lolos told Reuters. "The fact that someone inscribed the name on the pot shows that people were aware of the fact he had used this particular cave."
Lolos said his 15-member team chose to excavate it because it was the only one of three caves on the island that matched the historical description of the playwright's lair.

Excavations showed the 46 metre (150 foot) deep labyrinth of corridors and chambers had been used since pre-historic times. Artefacts showed neolithic people used it as a place to live and Romans as a place of worship.

"The fact that there are very few finds dating to the Classical era supports the idea that it was used by a single person," Lolos said. He said the ministry planned to open it to visitors after excavations were finished in two years.
